uncited: Single Scattering Models compute the radiance reaching the viewer by accounting for light that travels directly from a source to a volume and scatters exactly once toward the observer, while ignoring multiple scattering events and internal emission .
This method solves the problem of rendering volumetric effects like smoke or clouds efficiently by assuming that for low-density media, single scattering dominates the radiance contribution .

It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as the [Gradient-guided single scattering approximation](11126-gradient-guided-single-scattering-approximation.md), by its rigorous inclusion of volume attenuation and phase function integration in a two-pass framework, whereas other approximations may rely on gradient guidance or simplified shading rules .
All optical models in this family are derived from the conservation of energy for a differential cylinder of light passing through a medium .
It is described by the absorption coefficient $\sigma_a$ (units: $m^{-1}$) .
It is described by the emissive term $L_e(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega})$, representing radiance emitted per unit length .
It is split into *In-scattering* (light from other directions reflected into the view ray) and *Out-scattering* (light from the view ray reflected away) .
In most lighting calculations, out-scattering is folded into the **extinction** term because its net effect on the view ray is identical to absorption .
